The Digital Ceasefire & De-escalation Handbook provides a practical framework for mediators, negotiators, and affected communities to negotiate, draft, and implement ceasefire, de-escalation, and other agreements that constrain digital operations in conflict and other security contexts.

Developed in response to the accelerating digitalization of warfare, the Platform addresses the urgent need to confront hostile digital operations. Ceasefire agreements have traditionally overlooked the digital dimensions of conflict, leaving gaps in civilian protection and allowing unconstrained digital operations to take place.

The Platform addresses three interconnected dimensions of digital warfare: Internet Interference; Information Threats; and Cyber Attacks. It places the experiences and protection of conflict-affected populations at the center of its approach.

Grounded in International Law, including International Humanitarian Law, International Human Rights Law, and International Criminal Law, the Platform recognizes the challenges of applying existing legal frameworks to evolving digital threats. While Parties remain bound by their obligations under International Law, the Platform enables them to negotiate additional commitments to restrain and de-escalate digital operations that may otherwise be lawful.

At its core is the Digital Ceasefire & De-escalation Handbook, a living resource designed to evolve alongside technological developments, emerging threats, and lessons from practice. Rather than prescribing a single solution, the Handbook offers a flexible menu of model provisions that Parties can select, adapt, and combine to develop agreements tailored to different conflict and security contexts.

Through the Platform's [Build an Agreement function](#/builder), users can construct customized agreements using the Handbook's model provisions. The [Note to Users](#/handbook/s-note-to-users) provides useful background to constructing an Agreement. Alternatively, the [entire handbook](#/handbook) can be read and used here as a guide to support and contribute to existing negotiations.

### Background to the Platform

The [Digital Ceasefire & De-escalation Platform](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/projects/digital-ceasefire-and-de-escalation-handbook/) is an initiative of the [Human Rights Center](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/) at the University of California, Berkeley School of Law, and is co-led by Senior Research Fellow [Brett Solomon](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/people/brett-solomon/) and Executive Director [Betsy Popken](https://humanrights.berkeley.edu/people/betsy-popken/). The Handbook has been informed by research, consultations, and engagement with experts and practitioners working across conflict mediation and negotiation, international law, human rights, humanitarian protection, and digital technologies.

The initiative seeks to bridge the gap between the rapidly evolving realities of digital warfare and the practical tools available to those working to prevent conflict, reduce hostilities, protect civilians, and advance Digital Peace.

The Digital Ceasefire team is available to provide advice, technical assistance, briefings, training, and support to mediators, negotiators, civil society organizations, and others addressing the digital dimensions of conflict.

The full text of the Digital Ceasefire & De-escalation Handbook is available here, section by section, or it can be downloaded in full in [PDF format](#handbook-pdf). The Handbook guides users through the process of developing an Agreement, using the Platform's [Build an Agreement function](#/builder). We recommend starting with reading the [Note to Users](#/handbook/s-note-to-users) below. Sections 1.0 through 11.0 then provide model provisions that can be selected, adapted, and combined in [Build an Agreement](#/builder) to construct an Agreement tailored to different conflict and security contexts.

Use the Build an Agreement function to create an Agreement tailored to your specific conflict or security context. We recommend reading the [Note to Users](#/handbook/s-note-to-users) before you begin.

To get started, choose one of three approaches:

- **Build from scratch:** Select the provisions you wish to include from the left-hand column and add them to your Agreement in the right-hand column.
- **Start with the full Agreement:** Add all of the Handbook's model provisions to your Agreement, then remove those that are not relevant.
- **Use Handbook view:** Read the Handbook section by section and add provisions to your Agreement as you go.

Either way, once you have selected your provisions, you can edit and adapt the text in the right-hand column to reflect the specific circumstances, priorities, and commitments of the Parties.

Your Agreement is saved automatically in this browser, and you can come back to it at any time. You will find your saved Agreements in the Drafts box at the top left of the builder.

You can download your Agreement in various formats: Word, Markdown and PDF, by selecting the format in the Export drop down.

A few things to note:

- Terms that are defined will be included in the Definitions section, which you can add to.
- Relevant footnotes will also be included in the final Agreement.

sections.title: Preamble
sections.guidance:
Preambles typically include the purpose of the Agreement; the motivations of the parties; relevant principles, history, and values; and the context that informs the interpretation of the provisions.

The Preamble provides a broad menu of provisions that Parties may select, modify, or omit according to the context and purpose of their Agreement. Not all provisions are intended for inclusion by Parties.

Parties should distinguish between language that provides context, recognizes principles or marginalized groups, or expresses shared aspirations, and substantive commitments intended to guide conduct. Where the latter are included, Parties should consider corresponding operative and monitoring provisions.

An expansive Preamble may be appropriate in some contexts, while in others a shorter Preamble may better facilitate negotiation and Agreement. The provisions below are therefore options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may therefore include all of these provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: Entry into Force
sections.guidance:
Entry into force provisions define the exact time and date the Agreement begins, the conditions that must be satisfied before it begins, and/or the mechanism through which it becomes effective.

Prior to an Agreement entering into force, Parties typically establish mechanisms for addressing breaches to the Agreement, such as consultation, review, suspension, or termination, before the Agreement enters into force.

The provisions below are options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may therefore include all of the provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: Prohibited Digital Operations
sections.guidance:
This section is modeled after the Prohibited Acts section in a ceasefire Agreement, which identifies the specific actions the Parties agree to cease and therefore may not perform during the period the Agreement is in effect. Essentially, Prohibited Digital Operations are Digital Operations the Parties agree to cease under the Agreement.

If Parties are unable to agree to prohibit Digital Operations, they view cessation as infeasible or undesirable, or they wish to actively limit but not comprehensively cease certain activities, they can instead agree to de-escalate Digital Operations. In that case, Parties could instead use the term “De-escalated Digital Operations” and language such as “reduce” or "mitigate" or “de-escalate” instead of “cease” or “stop” or “prohibit.” Parties could then set a numerical or percentage threshold for De-escalation or set a frequency-based, severity-based, or impact-based threshold. For example, Parties could agree to reduce the number of Cyber Attacks or Internet Shutdowns over a specified period, limit the duration or geographic scope of such disruptions, reduce the scale of Information Interference campaigns, or establish measurable targets for reducing civilian harm. Such commitments could be time-bound, progressively strengthened, and subject to monitoring and verification to assess compliance and progress toward De-escalation. This Handbook is structured around Prohibited Digital Operations, but each provision can be adapted to be a De-escalated Digital Operation.

Such provisions vary in their level of detail. Some Agreements have broad prohibited acts, simply prohibiting the parties from using any kind of military force, while others provide a detailed list to make it very clear to the Parties what may constitute a breach.

This section first provides broad provisions the Parties may use to cease Prohibited Digital Operations against Civilian Objects, Military Objectives, and Dual-Use objects. The section is then divided into three categories so the Parties can choose provisions that are specific to their particular context: (1) Internet Interference; (2) Information Threats; and (3) Cyber Attacks.

Parties may have different reasons for prohibiting a Digital Operation under an Agreement, including the level of harm it may cause, the risk of escalation, or the threat it poses to a ceasefire or De-escalation process. However, provisions concerning Prohibited Digital Operations should be negotiated, agreed upon, and respected by all Parties.

In agreeing to Prohibited Digital Operations provisions, Parties should be aware of and distinguish between operations directed at Military Objectives and those directed at civilians and Civilian Objects, including civilian infrastructure and services. Parties should also consider that the immediate target may differ from the object or persons ultimately affected, and that harm may spread across interconnected systems, emerge over time, or extend beyond the intended target. Provisions may therefore address not only what may be targeted, but also the direct, indirect, and reasonably foreseeable harm that an operation may cause to Civilian Objects and/or the effect on Military Objectives.

Prohibited Digital Operations agreed to by the Parties does not necessarily mean that they are prohibited under International Law. Nothing in this Agreement shall be interpreted as diminishing the protections afforded under International Law.

Parties may agree to refrain from otherwise lawful Digital Operations in furtherance of restraint, De-escalation, confidence-building, or the cessation of hostilities.

The provisions below are options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may wish to add more specificity to the provisions based on their particular situation. Parties may include all of the provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: Internet Interference
sections.guidance:
These provisions seek to preserve the availability and integrity of the internet as essential to communication, access to information, and the functioning of society in times of Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, and Internal Disturbance.

Internet Interference can take many forms. It may be indiscriminate, affecting entire countries and populations. In other contexts, disruptions may be highly targeted, affecting specific regions, neighborhoods, or communities, including along ethnic, religious, or political lines. Interference may also vary in duration and severity, ranging from temporary Throttling or blocking of particular services or sites to prolonged or complete shutdowns.

Internet Interference can be identified through open-source monitoring, but determining its cause, attribution, and intent may be significantly more difficult. Monitoring mechanisms can therefore establish appropriate methodologies and evidentiary standards for assessing alleged violations and distinguishing deliberate disruption from technical failures or the effects of kinetic operations.

If Parties instead agree to limit or de-escalate Internet Interference, they can establish measurable targets, such as reducing the number or frequency of incidents by a specified percentage, limiting their duration or severity, or reducing their geographic scope or impact on civilians.

The provisions below are options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may therefore include all of the provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: Information Threats
sections.guidance:
These provisions aim to protect the integrity of the information environment by limiting coercive, deceptive, and manipulative information related practices that threaten public trust, democratic processes, and civilian protection in times of Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, and Internal Disturbance, including information operations that undermine the Agreement or are directed against the Parties to the Agreement. No provisions should be included in the Agreement that violate the rights of individuals, including their rights to freedom of expression, access to information, and privacy.

To strengthen the enforceability of an Agreement, particularly with respect to Misinformation, Disinformation, and Hate Speech, Parties should tailor the provisions in this section to identify and expressly prohibit specific narratives, content, or practices relevant to the conflict and security challenges they face. Parties may wish to narrow the prohibited Information Threats to a closed list of objectively verifiable acts that cause harm in their particular context. For example, if relevant, the Parties may agree to prohibit (1) fabricated official communications such as statements falsely attributed to the other Party's leadership or the Monitoring Commission; (2) false humanitarian information including announcements of corridors, safe zones, or evacuation routes that are false and issued with intent to deceive; (3) identified individual incitement such as content that names a specific individual and calls for violence against them.

Information Threats may occur in local, tribal, or Indigenous languages. Assessing alleged violations may require substantial linguistic, contextual, and technical expertise that may not be available in real time. Parties may therefore consider linguistic diversity and local cultural contexts when establishing monitoring and response mechanisms.

If Parties instead agree to limit or de-escalate Information Threats, they can establish measurable targets, such as reducing the number or frequency of incidents by a specified percentage, limiting their scale, reach, or severity of the threats, or establish thresholds to reduce their harmful impact on civilians.

The provisions below are options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may therefore include all of the provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: Interference with Humanitarian Information and Data
Cyber Attacks
sections.guidance:
These provisions prohibit hostile Cyber Operations used to gain unauthorized access to information, conduct Surveillance, and disrupt or manipulate Digital systems.

In the context of an Armed Conflict, not all such Cyber Operations constitute “attacks” under International Humanitarian Law; for example, Digital Surveillance or the use of Spyware does not necessarily constitute a Cyber Attack under International Humanitarian Law even if it is a hostile Cyber Operation.

States sometimes conduct Cyber Attacks against the military, or administrative or political infrastructure of another State in lieu of kinetic attacks. States also conduct Cyber Operations to disrupt criminal networks abroad as a routine part of law enforcement operations. For these reasons, Parties may be reluctant to accept a complete prohibition on all Cyber Operations. Instead, they may wish to focus on prohibiting or limiting the most harmful and destabilizing forms of cyber activity, particularly those affecting civilian populations and critical infrastructure.

Parties agreeing to cease Cyber Attacks should make clear in the Agreement that doing so does not enable any Party to conduct kinetic attacks. Parties should make clear that commitments to cease Cyber Attacks do not authorize or justify the commission of kinetic operations, and the Parties should consider how Digital and kinetic ceasefire commitments interact to prevent escalation across domains.

If Parties instead agree to limit or de-escalate Cyber Attacks, they can establish measurable targets, such as reducing the number or frequency of attacks by a specified percentage, limiting their scale, severity, or duration, or reducing their harmful impact on civilians and civilian infrastructure.

The provisions below are options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may therefore include all of the provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: Denial of Service (DoS) and Distributed Denial of Service Attacks (DDoS)
Weaponization of Digital Infrastructure and Systems
Third Parties
sections.guidance:
A Third Party is any person, group, organization, or other entity that becomes involved in the Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, or Internal Disturbance either by assisting one or more of the Parties or by engaging in it as a non-signatory actor. Parties may wish to include provisions in Section 4 to ensure that Third Parties do not undertake or otherwise circumvent any prohibition contained in this Agreement.

These provisions apply to all Prohibited Digital Operations set out in Section 3 and to the relevant Third Parties including Proxy Actors, Cyber Mercenaries, Third Party States, and Information and Technology Communications Companies included in the Agreement.

Parties often address the involvement of Third Parties in an Armed Conflict, either by agreeing to prohibit the actions of those under their control or by agreeing more broadly that the activities of all Proxy Actors shall be prohibited without assigning responsibility.

While the first option more precisely ties in the Parties to the Agreement, the second option may be easier for Parties to agree to. While Parties typically name the Proxy Actors over whom they have control, the Parties may instead choose to set a standard of control that can be applied by the Monitoring Commission. They may agree that the conduct of a specific Prohibited Digital Operation is attributable to a Party where that Party directed or exercised “effective control” over that specific operation (Nicaragua standard). Alternatively, the Parties may agree that every Prohibited Digital Operation conducted by an organized group may be attributable to a Party if that Party exercised “overall control” over the group at the time of the operation (Tadić standard), which may include financing and equipping the group or coordinating or assisting in the general planning of its activities.

These provisions are intended to establish commitments agreed between the Parties and should not be understood as modifying or replacing the applicable rules of attribution or State responsibility under International Law. While the Parties may agree to these commitments, it does not necessarily determine whether such conduct is attributable to a Party under International Law.

If Parties instead agree to limit or De-escalate Digital Operations by Third Parties, they can establish measurable targets, such as reducing the number or frequency of such operations by a specified percentage, limiting their scale, scope, or severity, or reducing their harmful impact on civilians and civilian infrastructure.

The provisions below are options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may therefore include all of the provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: Constructive Digital Operations
sections.guidance:
Ceasefire Agreements often include humanitarian provisions intended to protect and provide aid to refugees, internally displaced persons, humanitarian workers, prisoners of war, and other protected persons and non-combatants. Similar positive provisions can also be included in an Agreement which addresses the Digital components of Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, or Internal Disturbance. These may include connectivity, humanitarian information, defensive cybersecurity, Data protection, Confidence Building Measures, or other functions that Parties wish to provision.

The provisions below are options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may therefore include all of the provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: Digital Monitoring Commission
sections.guidance:
This section is modeled after monitoring commissions often included in ceasefire Agreements and includes provisions specific to the uniqueness and complexity of Digital Operations. Ceasefire Agreements sometimes create a commission which can have a range of roles with respect to the ceasefire. These can include: being responsible for information sharing between the parties to the Agreement and with the commission; monitoring the parties’ compliance with the terms of the Agreement; verifying any alleged breaches to the Agreement’s provisions; reporting on alleged and/or confirmed breaches; and assisting with dispute resolution between the Parties.

Monitoring commissions can hold the parties accountable for the acts they agree to cease or De-escalate and can act as a deterrent. Sometimes the Parties are unable to agree to implement a monitoring body, whether due to the difficulty of monitoring and verifying breaches, geopolitical factors, and/or resource constraints. While Agreements can be reached without a monitoring body, there would be no entity to hold the parties accountable for breaches to the Agreement. Monitoring can also be conducted by an existing United Nations or regional body mechanism. This section applies to situations of Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, and Internal Disturbance.

If Parties agree to De-escalate Digital Operations instead of ceasing them, the Monitoring Commission can fulfill its roles by evaluating potential breaches by a numerical or percentage threshold for frequency-based, severity-based, or impact-based threshold agreed by the Parties.

The provisions below are options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may therefore include all of the provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: Dissemination and Promotion of this Agreement
sections.guidance:
Ceasefire Agreements often include provisions requiring the parties to communicate the Agreement among the parties themselves, but also to inform the general public, Third Party actors, and the international community. If the appropriate stakeholders are not aware of the Agreement, there are likely to be violations of the Agreement’s terms and a breakdown in trust among the Parties.

These provisions apply to situations of Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, and Internal Disturbance. The provisions below are options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may therefore include all of the provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: External Support
sections.guidance:
Ceasefire Agreements typically require significant financial means to implement. Financial support can be secured in advance of the Agreement being signed and/or the Agreement can include provisions that call for commitments to provide financial support. Financial commitments also provide geopolitical weight behind the Agreement.

This section applies to Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, and Internal Disturbance. The provisions below are options and should be selected and adapted as appropriate. Parties may therefore include all of the provisions, just a few of them, or none at all.

sections.title: Signatures
sections.guidance:
Ceasefire Agreements usually include the signatures of representatives of the parties agreeing to the provisions of the Agreement. It is often helpful to include the signatures of Third Party witnesses and other Third Parties whose compliance and support may be necessary to ensure the Agreement’s effective implementation. Third Party signatures may include Information and Communication Technology Companies. Parties may also commit to being responsible for the actions of certain Proxy Actors.

Parties to this Agreement understand that Party representative signatures are required to bring the Agreement into force. Signatories must have the authority to conclude such an Agreement on behalf of the Party.

Third Parties serving as [mediators] [witnesses] [assisting in the implementation and monitoring of the Agreement] shall include their signatures to ensure compliance with this Agreement.

sections.title: Annex on Commitment to International Law

provisions.text: The Digital Ceasefire & De-escalation Handbook provides a framework and language that Parties and mediators can use to negotiate and mediate Digital Operations in Armed Conflicts, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances. All words that are capitalized in this Note to Users and in the Handbook are defined in the Definitions section of the Handbook.

The Handbook was drafted to reflect the increasing use of Digital technologies and capabilities by parties, ensuring that any Agreement binding Parties to cease or de-escalate prohibited acts, whether Digital or otherwise, can include language to address this reality.

The structure of this Handbook is modeled after and adapted from ceasefire Agreements, including provisions in sections titled Preamble; Entry into force; Prohibited Digital Operations; Third Parties; Constructive Digital Operations; Digital Monitoring Commission; Dissemination and Promotion of the Agreement; External Support; Definitions; and Signatories. Although ceasefire Agreements usually extend beyond International Law obligations, parties often acknowledge their legal responsibilities, so an Annex for Commitments to International Law is included, from which parties can draw language depending upon whether they are negotiating in the context of an Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activities, or Internal Disturbances.

The provisions in this Handbook are a menu of options, not a comprehensive model to be adopted in full. Parties may select, adapt, combine, or omit provisions according to the context, objectives, and scope of the situation. As outlined below, Agreements may take various forms: provisions may be incorporated into an Agreement that addresses the kinetic elements of a conflict, annexed to such an Agreement, or stand alone.
Prohibited Digital Operations

The Handbook uses the term Prohibited Digital Operations to refer to Digital Operations that the Parties agree to De-escalate or cease undertaking. The term is therefore defined by the commitments the Parties choose to include in their Agreement and may encompass Digital Operations in the context of an Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activities, or Internal Disturbances.

Importantly, describing an operation as “prohibited” under the Agreement does not imply that such operations are necessarily unlawful under International Law; rather, it reflects the specific restraints the Parties have agreed to observe. This may include Agreement to cease otherwise lawful Digital Operations as a measure of restraint, De-escalation, or confidence-building.

If Parties are unable to agree to prohibit Digital Operations, they view cessation as infeasible or undesirable, or they wish to actively limit but not comprehensively cease certain activities, they can instead agree to de-escalate Digital Operations. In that case, Parties could instead use the term “De-escalated Digital Operations” and language such as “reduce” or "mitigate" or “de-escalate” instead of “cease” or “stop” or “prohibit.” Parties could then set a numerical or percentage threshold for De-escalation or set a frequency-based, severity-based, or impact-based threshold. This Handbook is structured around Prohibited Digital Operations, but each provision in this Handbook can be adapted to instead focus on De-escalated Digital Operations.
Categories of Prohibited Digital Operations
This Handbook divides Prohibited Digital Operations into three categories as set out in Section 3:

1. Internet Interference, which the Parties may agree include Internet Shutdowns, Internet Infrastructure Attacks, Electronic Jamming, Third Party Internet Interference, and Humanitarian and Emergency Connectivity Disruptions;

2. Information Threats, which the Parties may agree include Misinformation and Disinformation, Manipulated Media, Inauthentic Behavior, Doxxing, Online Incitement to Violence, Hate Speech, Online Recruitment, Malicious Online Advertisements, Interference with Humanitarian Information and Data, Harassment of Journalists and Media, and Intimidating Diaspora;

3. Cyber Attacks, which the Parties may agree include Surveillance and Spyware, Hacking, Malware, Distributed Denial of Service Attacks, Phishing, Critical Infrastructure Attacks, and Weaponization of Digital Infrastructure and Systems.

As is typical of ceasefire Agreements, the Parties may agree to cease Prohibited Digital Operations against Military Objectives as well as Civilian Objects and Dual-Use Objects, even if not prohibited by International Law.

In addition to the categories of Prohibited Digital Operations, Section 5.0 provides an opportunity for the Parties to establish and agree upon a set of permissible or constructive commitments relating to connectivity, cyber defense, information dissemination, and other human rights and humanitarian protections.
Application of the Handbook to Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances

In the context of an Armed Conflict, this Handbook contains model language that may be incorporated into a ceasefire Agreement, appended as an annex to a broader ceasefire Agreement, or used to negotiate a standalone Digital ceasefire Agreement. Handbook provisions may also be adapted for use in comprehensive peace Agreements or other Agreements negotiated during the conduct of hostilities or as part of a broader peace process.

In situations of Grey Zone Activities or Internal Disturbances, where there is no Armed Conflict present, Parties may similarly wish to restrain, reduce, or cease specified Digital Operations. However, while Digital Operations may be ceased in Armed Conflicts, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances, a Ceasefire presupposes the existence of an Armed Conflict.

In the absence of Armed Conflict, Handbook provisions may instead be incorporated into other forms of Agreement, such as political Agreements, codes of conduct, or adopted as Confidence Building Measures (CBMs) aimed at cessation or De-escalation. They may also be drafted as memoranda of understanding, framework Agreements, or other shorter instruments focused on broad principles. This Handbook also includes provisions relevant to contexts which remain below the threshold of Armed Conflict. In such instances other forms of language will generally be more appropriate than ceasefire terminology.

Digital De-escalation or cessation may occur in Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances, and may involve a reduction in the intensity, frequency, scope, or end to Digital Operations.
Practical Challenges to Negotiating and Monitoring Digital Operations

Negotiating Digital Operations presents practical and technical challenges, which may affect how Parties agree to and implement certain provisions in this Handbook. Drafting requires careful consideration of what is to be prohibited and tracked and how such monitoring mechanisms can be designed to ensure specific prohibitions together with effective monitoring (see Section 6 for monitoring commission guidance).

Parties may, for instance, be reluctant to accept extensive restrictions on their Digital capabilities, submit to external monitoring, or reveal their capabilities for safety and security reasons. This may result in an Agreement that does not address some of the Digital Operations causing the greatest harm.

Attribution presents a further challenge: purported breaches, particularly Cyber Attacks and Information Threats, may not be attributable to a Party with complete certainty, including where Proxy Actors are involved. This Handbook addresses these challenges by enabling Parties to negotiate the degree of certainty required or designate that responsibility to a Digital Monitoring Commission and providing alternative approaches where attribution is not possible.

Digital technologies and capabilities will continue to evolve. Parties should therefore consider drafting the Agreement with sufficient flexibility to encompass evolving contexts as well as new and emerging technologies and forms of Digital Operations that produce effects comparable to those addressed by its provisions, even where they are not expressly identified.
Cessation or De-escalation?

The complete cessation of Prohibited Digital Operations may not always be immediately achievable or verifiable. Unlike some kinetic activities, Digital Operations may continue through anonymous or unattributed actors, Third Parties, or activity beyond the direct control of the Parties. Parties should therefore consider defining what meaningful restraint and De-escalation would look like given the range of actors in the particular context.

Provisions can be tailored accordingly. If the goal is cessation, Parties may identify the specific sources or types of Prohibited Digital Operations to be addressed. They may also focus on new or context-specific actions, allowing commitments to evolve in response to new Prohibited Digital Operations identified by the Monitoring Commission. The Parties may decide to focus their negotiations on reducing or ceasing Digital Operations which produce the most harm, whether kinetic or otherwise, to civilians, vulnerable communities, public infrastructure and data, or the military.

These approaches can provide practical indicators of progress while preserving the ultimate goal of ending Prohibited Digital Operations. Parties may establish appropriate benchmarks, reporting periods, and methods of verification in the Agreement.
Standards of Restraint

The provisions in this Handbook often provide a high standard of restraint. Where Parties may be unwilling or unable to agree to a maximalist prohibition, they may wish to adopt narrower commitments aimed at reducing or De-escalating particular Digital Operations. For instance, Parties may agree to prohibit a certain scale of breaches rather than one-off breaches; to assess and report on the harmful effects of breaches rather than only the number and type of breaches; and to Digitally track and self-report their own breaches for public awareness.
Specificity to Context

Provisions in this Handbook are designed to be adaptable to any Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, and Internal Disturbance. Parties should consider drafting more targeted provisions by identifying specific forms of conduct, content, or narratives relevant to their context, and providing additional parameters, such as time, place, or actors, to more clearly define the Parties’ commitments. Parties may find certain provisions appropriate to end active fighting, while more may be longer term, normative items that are appropriate for a future Agreement.
Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Companies

Because Information and Communication Technology (ICT) Companies’ products and services may be used to facilitate or otherwise contribute to Cyber Attacks, Internet Interference, and Information Threats, ICT Companies often play a significant role in the Digital dimensions of Armed Conflicts, Grey Zone Activities, and Internal Disturbances without being formal Parties to the Agreement. While ICT Companies are often important stakeholders in efforts to reduce harm, establishing shared responsibilities and securing meaningful cooperation can be complex given their diverse mandates, business models, and regulatory obligations.

Some experts believe that in exceptional circumstances, an ICT Company may become a Party to an Armed Conflict, depending on its conduct and the applicable legal thresholds. Where an ICT Company is state-owned, Prohibited Digital Operations committed under the direction or control of that Party may be attributable to that Party, and therefore any such acts attributed to State-owned, State-controlled, or otherwise authorized ICT Companies breach Parties’ commitments under the Agreement.

This Handbook provides provisions that allow ICT Companies to commit to ending the use of their products and services in the commission of Prohibited Digital Operations; to contribute their services to monitoring the Agreement; and to be signatories to the Agreement.

ICT Companies can also adopt separate commitments or codes of conduct, or serve as implementation partners. Such commitments may be voluntary or legally binding, depending on the nature of the instrument. The Agreement should clearly identify the nature of these commitments and, where appropriate, the specific ICT Companies to which they apply.
Emerging Technologies

This is a forward-looking Handbook that is designed to provide Parties with language that can be included for current technologies, but the purpose of the Agreement is a cessation or De-escalation of the effects and consequences of Prohibited and De-escalated Digital Operations, regardless of the specific technology or system used. Accordingly, Parties may wish for the Agreement to apply, where relevant, to new and emerging technologies and forms of Digital Operations that produce effects comparable to those addressed by its provisions, even where such technologies or operations are not expressly identified or enumerated in the Agreement. In which case, Parties should include language to that effect.

The Handbook does not include a separate Prohibited Digital Operation focused on Artificial Intelligence (AI), recognizing that AI is regularly used in connection with Internet Interference, Information Threats, Cyber Attacks, and other Digital Operations addressed throughout the Handbook. As the use and capabilities of AI continue to grow, the Handbook treats AI as a cross-cutting technology rather than a distinct category of Prohibited Digital Operations.
International Law

Because ceasefire Agreements often reference and reaffirm the Parties’ obligations under International Law, the Handbook includes an Annex on Commitments to International Law in section 11. Its provisions may be incorporated into the Preamble, included throughout the Agreement, or retained as an Annex as set out here.

While the Handbook provisions draw upon existing International Law obligations, they also extend beyond it. Some provisions reflect legal obligations for the Parties (with the applicable legal basis set out in the footnotes), whereas others provide model commitments that Parties may voluntarily agree to adopt as part of a ceasefire or De-escalation Agreement, including commitments to refrain from conduct that would otherwise be lawful. Other provisions may contribute to the development of emerging norms or the progressive development of International Law.

The inclusion of a provision in the Handbook should not, by itself, be understood as indicating that the conduct it addresses is required or prohibited under existing International Law. At the same time, users should note that Parties remain subject to applicable International Law regardless of whether they sign an Agreement and the Parties cannot use the Agreement to contract out of their legal duties and obligations.

In situations of Armed Conflict, International Humanitarian Law (IHL) provides the specific legal framework governing the conduct of hostilities, while International Human Rights Law (IHL) continues to apply as relevant without overriding it. In situations of Grey Zone Activity or Internal Disturbance, where International Humanitarian Law does not apply, International Human Rights Law provides the primary applicable legal framework in addition to International Criminal Law (ICL) in narrow circumstances. Users should also be aware that the relationship between the bodies of law can be complex and at times difficult to navigate.

This Annex takes into consideration the International Law obligations applicable to a Party depending on the nature of the Party (e.g. a State Party or non-State Party) and the context under which the security challenge arises, including Armed Conflict, Grey Zone Activity, or Internal Disturbances.
Kinetic and Digital Dimensions of Conflict

Digital and kinetic operations should not be understood as entirely separate spheres of conflict, given they often occur simultaneously and can be operationally integrated. For example, Cyber Attacks may precede or accompany a kinetic strike; Information Threats may support Military Objectives on the battlefield; and Internet Shutdowns may be enacted just following military strikes on a city.

Users should consider this relationship when negotiating and implementing a Digital ceasefire or De-escalation Agreement. Commitments to ceasing or de-escalating Digital Operations should not be interpreted or implemented in ways that facilitate, enable, or provide cover for prohibited kinetic activity, nor should restraint in one domain be exploited to intensify hostilities in another. For example, a Party should not use a cessation or reduction of Cyber Attacks to create an operational advantage for increased kinetic attacks, nor should a Party exploit restored communications, networks, or Digital Infrastructure to identify or attack opposing forces or civilians.

Equally, a kinetic attack should not be treated as justification for breaching commitments relating to Digital Operations. Where the Parties intend violations or developments in one domain to have consequences for commitments in another, those consequences should be expressly agreed rather than assumed.

Parties should therefore coordinate between Digital and broader ceasefire and De-escalation arrangements where both are present. This could be achieved through common implementation and monitoring mechanisms; procedures for addressing operations that combine Digital and kinetic elements; protections against exploiting restored Digital services or infrastructure for hostile purposes; and mechanisms for managing alleged violations without triggering reciprocal escalation across domains.

Ultimately, the purpose of an Agreement is cessation or De-escalation. An Agreement’s provisions should be interpreted and implemented in a manner that reduces opportunities for Parties to shift activities between Digital and kinetic means and prevents restraint in one domain from being exploited in another.
Freedom of Expression

Nothing in this Agreement should be interpreted or applied to unduly restrict lawful expression, including political speech, journalism, satire, or legitimate criticism. All provisions should be narrowly tailored and applied consistently with International Human Rights Law, including Article 19 of the ICCPR.
Background to this Handbook

The text of this Handbook is based on a combination of academic research, dozens of primary source interviews, and a review of historical and existing ceasefire and peace Agreements. Consultations with technical experts, diplomats, mediators, advisors, people on the ground in conflicts, and Parties currently or previously engaged in dialogue and mediation processes is ongoing to ensure that the provisions proposed directly meet the needs of existing conflict and security challenges.
The Handbook was developed with reference to the Public International Law and Policy Group’s Ceasefire Drafter’s Handbook.

The authors recommend that Parties using this Handbook engage with technical experts who understand the Digital dimensions of the security challenge, the technologies being used, and how such uses might be monitored and verified. The authors also recommend scoping the full range of acts, both Digital and non-Digital, so Parties can address both or complement existing negotiations. Finally, the authors recommend the Parties work with lawyers to understand which acts of the other Party are already prohibited by International Law.

State Parties agree that their national intelligence agencies will share with the Monitoring Commission, or provide upon its request, information regarding Information Threats from their territories and Information Threats committed by Proxy Actors.

State Parties agree that their Computer Emergency Response Teams (CERTS) and Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTS) will share with the Commission, or provide upon its request, technical information regarding potential Cyber Attacks from their territories and Cyber Attacks committed by Proxy Actors, but may avoid attributing Cyber Attacks to a particular Party or Proxy Actor.

State Parties agree that representatives from their [CERTS and CSIRTS], [national intelligence agencies], [and national telecommunications and Digital regulatory bodies] shall participate in the Monitoring Commission to better facilitate information sharing.
The Parties agree to share information on a timely basis and preserve the privacy of information shared with or by the Monitoring Commission or other Parties.
The Parties agree to Digitally track and self-report any potential breaches to the Agreement of their own to the Monitoring Commission.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may {{o-request}} that the Parties provide access to the Commission to {{o-certain-systems-to-allow}}.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for monitoring compliance with this Agreement.
The Parties agree that monitoring means observing and recording events or actions related to this Agreement without making formal judgments about the Parties’ compliance with this Agreement.

The Parties understand that the Monitoring Commission will monitor potential breaches of the Agreement to the extent possible, recognizing that the level of certainty will depend on the type of breach (Internet Interference, Information Threat, or Cyber Attack), the information available about the possible breach, the technical capacity of the monitors, and the good faith of the Parties in providing relevant information.

The Parties authorize the Monitoring Commission to establish a mechanism by which Parties and non-parties can safely and anonymously report potential breaches of this Agreement. Non-parties may include civil society organizations, independent experts, international actors, and affected civilians.
The Parties agree that the Commission shall be responsible for establishing a process and timeline to notify the Parties of any Party’s perceived breaches to the Agreement.

The Parties agree that as part of its responsibility to monitor breaches to the Agreement, the Commission may request that Information and Communication Technology Companies provide information designed to help monitor breaches. Such requests may include, but are not limited to, information on: Cyber Attacks using a company’s tools or infrastructure; a Party to the Agreement demanding the company enact an Internet Shutdown; a Party’s or Proxy Actor’s use of a social media or communications platform for Online Incitement to Violence. In the case of Information Threats, the Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may {{o-require}} that a social media or communications platform preserve evidence. The Monitoring Commission may also use Information and Telecommunications Companies products and services to help attribute and verify potential breaches to the Agreement.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may request the technical support of ICT Companies for the purposes of monitoring the Agreement.

The Parties agree that as part of its responsibility to monitor breaches to the Agreement, the Monitoring Commission may request that Third Party States provide evidence of breaches with the Commission.
The Parties call upon ICT Companies with evidence of breaches of this Agreement to share that evidence with the Monitoring Commission.
The Parties call on Third Party States with evidence of breaches of this Agreement, to share that evidence with the Monitoring Commission.
The Parties agree that as part of its responsibility to monitor breaches to the Agreement, the Commission may request cooperation from Third Parties including Third Party States and ICT Companies.
The Parties agree to monitor their own compliance with the Agreement and to notify the Monitoring Commission of their own potential breaches to its provisions.
The Parties agree that if necessary, the Monitoring Commission may investigate alleged breaches through other means (e.g. interviews, open source investigations).
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may monitor the scale of alleged breaches as opposed to or in addition to each individual breach.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may monitor the harms of Prohibited Digital Operations allegedly committed by the Parties as opposed to or in addition to the breaches themselves.

The Parties urge the Monitoring Commission to understand local languages for the purpose of monitoring Information Threats to be able to adequately understand and assess the drivers of violence and social tension.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for examining and verifying whether allegations of breaches reported to or observed by the Monitoring Commission are indeed breaches.

The Parties agree that examination and verification means assessing and confirming whether the Parties are complying with this Agreement based on information observed or obtained by the Monitoring Commission or provided to the Monitoring Commission.

The Parties understand that to address instances where the Monitoring Commission is unable to verify and attribute potential breaches with absolute certainty, the Monitoring Commission will set percentage confidence thresholds disclosed to the Parties in advance (e.g. 80%) for each potential type of breach (e.g. Distributed Denial of Service) to be attributed to a particular Party. The Parties understand this percentage confidence threshold is likely to vary based on whether the breach concerns Internet Interference, Information Threats, or Cyber Attacks, and based on the incident and information available, and that breaches are only attributable up to that threshold.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission may use the products and services of Information and Telecommunications Companies to help attribute and verify potential breaches to the Agreement, where possible.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible, upon verifying a breach, for determining whether a Party, civilian, or other non-Party has legal or other recourse.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for reporting all verified breaches. The Parties understand this may result in a significant lag between an incident and a Commission finding, during which time the Parties shall refrain from publicly accusing one another.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for initially reporting all potential breaches to the Agreement. The Parties understand that reporting potential breaches may risk damaging a Party’s reputation before the Commission has confirmed the allegation, and the Parties shall not escalate their Prohibited Digital Operations before a Commission finding.

The Parties agree that reporting means sharing information about {{o-verified}} breaches of this Agreement with the public – using a structured, impartial, and evidence-based format that balances transparency, neutrality, and the protection of sensitive information. The Parties understand these reports are essential for documenting compliance, informing the public, and preventing escalation.
The Monitoring Commission may use Third Party evidence and Information and Communications Technology Company tools to report on {{o-verified}} breaches to the Agreement.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for reporting on the harms caused by Prohibited Digital Operations.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission will provide technical support and good offices to help resolve technical, operational, and political disputes between the Parties to this Agreement and provide best practices to the Parties.
If the Parties have questions about what constitutes a breach to the provisions of this Agreement, they can reach out to the Monitoring Commission for clarification.
The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission will hold consultations on grievances and concerns with the Parties [every six months]. The Parties agree to submit their allegations in advance.
The Parties agree that any Party can request that the Monitoring Commission suspend the Agreement if that Party believes another Party has materially breached the Agreement.

The Parties agree that the Monitoring Commission is responsible for determining and providing advance notice on the consequences for a Party’s breach to the Agreement. For instance, the Commission may require a Party’s appearance before guarantor States, communicate a formal statement of censure to the UN Secretary-General, issue a formal warning identifying the breach and requiring corrective action within a specified timeframe, or refer the Party for sanctions consideration.
The Parties agree that the announcement of this Agreement shall be disseminated by the Parties through command channels with written orders requiring compliance.

The Parties agree that the announcement of this Agreement and its provisions will be communicated to the civilian population in clear, accessible, and understandable formats, via print, radio, electronic media, social media, community networks, and all other possible means of communication. Announcements will be made in all relevant languages and translated as needed. Any significant updates to the Agreement made by the Parties must also be communicated.

The Parties agree to disseminate the announcement of this Agreement to all relevant Third Parties, including Proxy Actors, Third Party States, other States, and other actors who should be aware of the Agreement or may assist in monitoring the terms of the Agreement.

The Parties agree to communicate to their personnel, Proxy Actors, relevant Third Parties, the civilian population, civil society organizations, and the international community that the failure to comply with this Agreement is likely to result in renewed Prohibited Digital Operations and the breakdown of trust between the Parties and possibly violations of International Law.

The Parties agree to disseminate the announcement of this Agreement to and engage with Information and Communication Technology Companies and company Boards to promote compliance with and support for this Agreement.

The Parties shall provide accurate and up to date information concerning this Agreement to the media and shall not interfere with the dissemination of information about this Agreement. The Parties shall take steps to prevent dissemination of distorted or manipulated information about this Agreement.
The Parties shall give notice of this Agreement to the appropriate international and regional organizations.

The Parties welcome the commitment(s) of [financial supporter 1], [financial supporter 2], [financial supporter 3] to contributing the following monetary amount(s) to help implement this Agreement and to finance the Monitoring Commission.

The Parties call upon [financial supporter 1], [financial supporter 2], [financial supporter 3] to provide the necessary resources in the following monetary amount(s) to help implement this Agreement and to finance the Monitoring Commission.

The Parties welcome the commitment(s) of [State 1], [State 2], [State 3] to use their technical capabilities to help monitor certain terms of this Agreement in collaboration with the Monitoring Commission.
